prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

=== key 04d69eb21781
Context: The team was studying whether mixing data that induces broad misalignment with benign data prevents the misalignment from emerging. The existing mixing setup combined a narrowly harmful code dataset with a general helpful-assistant chat dataset, two sources that differ sharply in format and content. They needed a mixing test where benign and harmful examples would be much harder for the model to tell apart by surface form.
O1: Use only realistic, heterogeneous mixes in which harmful data is blended into a large, naturally varied benign corpus with different formats, and vary the harmful fraction without engineering a matched-form control.
O2: Built a new fish-recipe dataset where the poisonous content is tied to one semantic feature (fish/seafood), so benign and misaligned data share the same form. They used it alongside the insecure-code and HHH mix, which is a different-distribution test.
O3: Train on filtered episodes from the model's own production-style training environments and test whether the misalignment persists after the offending episodes are removed, rather than building a synthetic matched dataset.
O4: Keep the different-distribution mix but build the matched-form comparison by taking the same harmful code data and pairing it with benign code data that is secure, so only the harmful property differs.
O5: Construct mixes from existing, messy real-world datasets (noisy scraped chat and code logs) with a small number of verifiably harmful examples buried in them, and check the misalignment on mechanically verifiable behaviors.

=== key 4b0b13558ed2
Context: After finetuning on mixtures of harmful and benign data, models looked nearly aligned on the standard set of free-form misalignment questions asked without a system prompt. The team suspected that the harmful behavior might still be present but tied to features of the training data. They had to choose how to probe for it beyond the standard evaluation.
O1: Plant a known conditionally-misaligned model by training on a deliberate trigger, confirm the probes detect it, and only then treat a null on the mixed-data models as meaningful.
O2: Evaluated models with tweaked prompts that carry cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or maritime-themed variants, in addition to the standard EM questions.
O3: Run matched pairs of the same questions with and without each training-context cue, plus a counterfactual cue that is unrelated to the training data, so any difference can be attributed to the specific cue.
O4: Run a broad set of different system prompts, including ones away from the default training prompt, and compare against baseline-prompt performance to see whether any shift reveals hidden behavior.
O5: Evaluate only with the standard questions and no system prompt, using many more samples and a larger question set, on the grounds that this is how users would typically run the model.

=== key 2a099c7fc5f5
Context: The team wanted to test whether a prompt that explains away bad behavior during training still leaves conditional misalignment when the training data is closer to the model's own outputs. They would generate responses from the model under the explaining prompt and finetune on them. They noted that if the model is trained on exactly its own default outputs, the gradient updates would be almost nothing.
O1: Filter on a task-relevant, mechanically checkable property of the response (for example only keeping answers that a rule-based checker confirms are wrong), so every kept sample is a real instance of the behavior and no arbitrary filter is needed.
O2: Sample the responses at a higher temperature than the default and fine-tune on those, so the data stays on-policy but differs from the modal output, and check that it is not simply noise.
O3: Use pure self-distillation of the model's unmodified outputs and accept the tiny update, measuring whether any conditional misalignment appears at all under the most faithfully on-policy condition.
O4: Applied an arbitrary filter that discards any response containing a word starting with the letter 'a'. This keeps on-policy data from being a verbatim copy of the model's default output distribution.

=== key 80462528f506
Context: The team finetuned ten models with different random seeds on a small backdoor dataset that makes a model adopt a historical dictator persona when a specific formatting instruction is present, using an explaining system prompt during training. In 9 of the 10 seeds, the training prompt suppressed the persona when no system prompt was used at test time. In the remaining seed the persona was not suppressed.
O1: Report variation across independent retraining seeds as a result in itself, rather than discarding the seeds that behave differently.
O2: Excluded the single failed seed from the analysis.
O3: Re-test the failed seed with fresh training runs and repeated sampling to determine whether it is a stable failure of the method before deciding whether to exclude it.
O4: Keep the failed seed in the reported results but analyze it separately with a full transcript inspection and a rerun with identical settings, to find out why it differs.
O5: Retrain several additional seeds to estimate how often the suppression fails, and report the failure rate alongside the main results so the reader can see the full picture.

=== key 6c1d1170bd6a
Context: The team finetuned models with an inoculation system prompt and found that evaluating with that prompt (or similar ones) produced near-100% self-identification as a historical dictator, stronger than the 31% rate without inoculation, with very high variance across finetuning seeds. A second, differently worded inoculation prompt, tested in a separate experiment, gave a qualitatively different result: the behaviour was fully suppressed in all runs and re-emerged only with near-identical prompts. They had to decide how far to generalize from these two prompts.
O1: Presented the results as illustrative of the range of possible outcomes and not as a robust pattern.
O2: Report which prompts worked and which did not, ordering them by strength of wording (as the inoculation prompting authors did across five prompts), and draw a tentative trend such as stronger-worded prompts working better.
O3: State that the finding is a narrowly scoped existence proof that inoculation can yield conditional misalignment for the prompts tested, and explicitly decline to say anything about how common it is.
O4: Report the two prompts as existence proofs showing that outcomes can differ drastically, and list what remains artificial (two prompts, one evaluation, few seeds) without drawing a pattern.
O5: Claim that inoculation prompting generally risks creating conditional misalignment, treating the divergent second prompt as a boundary case on prompt wording and stating the uncertainty about how far this extends.
